paras: In Chapter 5 we saw that memory needs grammar. Defining what to remember is not enough; when several people read and write the same graph, the memory needs common rules.
Once memory begins to have structure, another question appears. How should we look at it?
We can view memory as a list. But a list shows individual items without making their relationships easy to see at a glance.
A graph has relationships. Those relationships need a space in which people can read them.
beats.claim: A view does not create a new graph. It looks at the same graph through a different question.

paras: Imagine a project with hundreds of concepts, records, and decisions. Search can find individual items.
But understanding where a decision began, what record supported it, and which later decisions followed it requires more than a page of search results.
One view shows surrounding connections. Another shows overall structure. Another shows the flow of time.
These are not different graphs. They are windows through which the same memory can be read from different directions.
Where the decision began, what supported it, and what followed from it are three questions a result list answers one row at a time.
People are accustomed to understanding connected information spatially. We perceive nearby things as related, and distant things as belonging to different areas.
That does not mean spatial position always represents real meaning accurately.
So Vinc does not try to reproduce the physical world as a map. Space here is a representation for reading graph structure.
The important question is not whether the layout is beautiful, but whether the same layout communicates the same meaning consistently from the same graph.
The layout is doing work either way; the only question is whether the work is repeatable.

beats.h: The Same Memory Stays in the Same Place
paras: A force-directed layout that produces a new arrangement on every pass may look natural, but it makes spatial memory impossible.
If a concept is in the upper left today and the lower right tomorrow, people cannot learn the space itself.
So the coordinates are not decoration. Layout should be reproducible derived state from the graph: the same input produces the same arrangement, and changes in the graph change the space accordingly.
The space does not move randomly. It moves with the structure of memory.
beats.claim: Within one graph, the same memory should be in the same place.

beats.h: More Than One Kind of Time
paras: Once we talk about space, time appears. And when we record a memory, when may not be a single question.
Suppose an event happened in 2020 and we recorded it in 2026. The time of the event and the time we began remembering it are different.
World time is the time in the world the memory describes. Graph time is the time that memory began to exist in the graph.

Combining them into one timestamp loses information. Recording a past event today does not mean the event happened today, and the fact that the record entered the graph today is itself part of the history.
beats.claim: When something happened and when we began remembering it are different questions.

beats.h: Time Changes What a Relationship Means
paras: Time is not merely a label. It lets us understand the order of decisions and events, and consider which memories could have influenced a later judgment.
If decision A existed before decision B, and B was made on the basis of A, the two have more than a link between them. They have an order.
When graph relationships and temporal relationships are read together, a causal structure appears.
Two things happening in sequence is not the same claim as one causing the other, and the graph has to be able to say which it means.

beats.h: Physics as a Lens, Not a Copy
paras: Relativistic spacetime gives events a past and a future and, under the constraint that influence cannot travel faster than light, regions that can be causally connected. The light cone is an intuitive picture of that.
Vinc is not implementing physics.
It borrows the concept as a way to think about which memories can be causally close to which others.
So physics does not define the laws here. It provides one lens for reading the graph.
Representing relationships in space and time does not mean everything has to become a number.
If there is no evidence for how one day should correspond to a distance in the graph, there is no reason to invent a figure for it. That number would be a designer's assumption, not data.
Likewise, a layout that looks Gaussian does not prove a Gaussian distribution exists behind it.
Borrow structures where they help, but do not invent meanings that are not present. Something can look plausible without having any semantic evidence behind it.
The space itself may now seem like the important thing. But space is not the source of memory.
The graph holds the structure. Space represents that structure so people can read it.
Whether we see the graph in three dimensions, in two, or along a timeline, we should still be reading the same graph.
This is the separation of view and source. Space helps us understand memory; it cannot replace the evidence of memory.
beats.claim: Changing the view must not change the memory.

beats.label: 6.close
paras: We distinguished what to remember, made a grammar for recording it, connected the relationships, and made the graph readable through space and time.
But memory does not act by itself. Someone has to read it, find what matters to the question at hand, follow the relevant relationships, and sometimes propose new memory.
